title: Korach: not for heaven's sake (Avot 5:17)
hookLine: the Mishnah names Korach's quarrel as the dispute not for heaven's sake
tomorrow: Korach: Moses falls on his face

cards: Some arguments are over by Friday, and nobody remembers what they were about. Others are still being studied, word by word, long after everyone in them has died.

The Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, sorts disputes into two piles, and gives each pile one example. For the good pile, two teachers whose schools disagreed again and again.
For the other pile, the rebel we met yesterday: Korach.

teach.b: Here's the teaching, in paraphrase. Every dispute that is for the sake of heaven will in the end endure. Every dispute that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure.
Which dispute was for the sake of heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not?
The dispute of Korach and all his company.
The Hebrew phrase is l'shem shamayim, for the name of heaven: an argument whose goal is the truth, not the person arguing.
Hillel and Shammai each left a school of students, and the two schools argued over question after question of Jewish law.
The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both schools speak the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel's school. The reason it gives isn't that they were cleverer.

They were patient and humble, they taught the other school's view along with their own, and they even mentioned Shammai's view first. Those arguments are still printed and studied today. That's what endure means.
Now look at the other half of the line. It doesn't say the dispute of Korach and Moses.
It says Korach and his company. Commentators noticed. In their reading, Moses wasn't fighting for himself at all.
And some add that Korach's allies each wanted something different, so a fight that's about winning ends up turning on itself.
Some teachers draw a simple test from this: in an argument for heaven's sake, you'd be glad if the other side turned out right, because then the truth won.

how: By custom, Pirkei Avot is studied a chapter at a time on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover, and in some communities through the summer, so this teaching about arguments comes around again and again.

o: the teacher whose school lost most debates to Hillel
the judge who settles disputes in a Jewish court
the rebel the Mishnah names for a dispute that won't last

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.

s: the Mishnah's example is the dispute of Korach and Moses
it says Korach and all his company. Moses isn't named as a side.
the Talmud says the law follows Hillel's school partly because they mentioned Shammai's view first
they were patient and humble, and taught both views.
an argument for heaven's sake ends with one side forgotten
it endures: Hillel and Shammai's arguments are still studied.

games.q: you're deep in an argument and suddenly realize the other person has a good point. what do you do?
o: change the subject before anyone notices.
say it out loud: that's a good point.
find a new argument so you still win.
games.why: the Talmud praises Hillel's school for teaching Shammai's view, even mentioning it first. an argument for heaven's sake is glad when the truth shows up, whoever brings it.

practice: Bring to mind someone you disagree with, about anything, large or small, and find the strongest thing they've said; put it into words as fairly as they would, maybe better.
Then ask one quiet question: if they turned out to be right, could I live with that? You don't have to change your mind, only notice which pile this argument belongs in.

wordCard.voice: Korach. The rebel the Mishnah chose as its example of a dispute not for heaven's sake, set beside Hillel and Shammai, whose arguments endure.

orig.note: Hebrew: for the sake of heaven, literally for the name of heaven.

carryVoice: Your line: not for heaven's sake. The arguments that last are about the truth. Day four hundred fifty-two, done.
